text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our board meeting of September 10th, 2024, and we're going to begin our meeting as we always do, which is to recognize any individuals that, sadly, we want to keep in our thoughts and prayers, and after those intentions, we'll all rise for a moment of silence, and the board's been away for a couple weeks, so there might be a number of these folks we want to recognize before we rise, and I'm going to begin just by mentioning a few pivotal members of our community that sadly we've lost since the

last time we met, starting with Lou Glickfield. Lou was the founder of Marlow Furniture, which if you live in this area, you certainly know Marlow Furniture, if for no other reason because of their radio ads. But he was instrumental in starting that family-owned business. Over the years, Marlow Furniture was named a top 50 retailer by Furniture Today and received numerous accolades from industry groups. He was married to his wife, Marilyn, for 71 years and has survived by four children, five grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren. Outside of his business

interests, Lou and his wife, Marilyn, always gave back to their community, have been very philanthropic over the years, establishing the Glickfield Family Foundation to support numerous regional and international charities, including the Anti-Defamation League, the Whitman Walker Clinic, Hadassah Hospital in Israel, and World Central Kitchen, among many other philanthropic efforts of Lou Glickfield and his family. So if we could remember him in our thoughts and prayers.

Secondly, sad to announce the passing of Gay Shane. Those of us certainly in the Richmond Highway Corridor, New Gage Shane Well. She passed away on August 15th at the age of 85, is survived by seven children and stepchildren, 17 grandchildren, and 13 great-grandchildren.

And she was all about her family. We knew her, of course, because she advocated on many causes before this board. She was a longtime member, board member and chairman of MVLE, which many of us are familiar with in the work that they do for children, in particular adults and children with disabilities.

She was also a board member of Operation Renewed Hope Foundation. Where I got to know her also is I am a board member of Operation Renewed Hope Foundation, which helps homeless veterans find shelter in homes. And Gay was a pivotal part of the South County, but also of all of Fairfax County.

I also want to pass along the sad news to members of our county family that have passed away. Jonathan Wood was president and deputy chief of the Fair Oaks Volunteer Fire and Rescue Department, Company 421.

Jonathan served over 50 years as a volunteer with FCFRD. He passed away peacefully on the evening of Thursday, August 22nd, leaving behind a legacy of dedication, leadership, and service that has deeply impacted our department and the broader Fairfax County community.

And certainly among the ranks of our professional firefighters and volunteer firefighters, everybody knew who Jonathan Wood was and the just outstanding service he provided to our community. And finally, Ed Kilgore. Ed served in the county's Department of Public Safety Communications for over 20 years.

With the skills of teletype and fire dispatch, his quick wit and sharp mind made him a cornerstone of our fire dispatch operations, where he was fondly known as the voice of 4B on the B-day shift. Beyond his professional contributions, Ed filled his days with laughter, delivering puns and endless dad jokes, and left a lasting impression with all of us and was shared with me that whenever anyone asked Ed Kilgore, how are you doing, his response was either it's another day in paradise or finer than a frog's hair split three ways.

So I'm sure Ed would really appreciate hearing us get a laugh at him at his expense, but he was always quite the professional, but always quite the person who could generate a laugh in what could be a very stressful job, certainly over at DPSC.

And so if we could keep Ed and his family in our thoughts and prayers as well, that would be appreciated. And at this time, happy to recognize my other colleague, Supervisor Herity. Let me start by thank you for recognizing Jonathan Wood. He was a clearly trained generation of our firefighters and EMTs and was best known for making the rounds of Santa in the fire truck, and he'll be missed for a lot of reasons.

Also would like to, unfortunately, recognize the passing of former First Lady Roxanne Gilmore on August 7th. Many know her through her husband of 47 years, former governor of Virginia, Jim Gilmore. She was a lifelong teacher, both in public schools and an assistant professor at Randolph-Macon College.

Her interest in a variety of subject areas influenced her to create the Commonwealth of Knowledge webpage for educators across the state and the Conexus for Children's Vision program, helping to provide eye examinations and glasses to children in public schools.

As First Lady, she led the restoration of the Governor's Mansion and archaeological work at the historical sites like Jamestown. Just ask that we keep the Gilmores in our thoughts and prayers. Also, the passing of retired Fairfax County Fire and Rescue Master Technician Bob Upchurch, who passed away suddenly on August 12th.

He's the father of firefighter Jason Upchurch, who was assigned to Fairfax County Station 25B shift, and the son of retired Captain Donovan Upchurch of the Alexandria Fire Department. He joined the Fire and Rescue Department in 1987, remained a value member even after his retirement in 2021.

He was known for meticulous attention to detail and his unmatched mechanical aptitude. He dedicated countless hours to researching, writing, and teaching the art of being an apparatus technician. His legacy lives on through the personnel he trained, the apparatus he helped design, and through his son's dedication to the Fairfax County Fire and Rescue Department.

I ask we keep the Upchurch family and our fire and rescue family in our thoughts and prayers. Thank you, Supervisor Herity. Supervisor Stork. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I appreciate recognizing two people that really were phenomenally important to the community.

First and foremost is somebody who I got to know well, Marcia Manning. From 2005 to 2012, Marcia served as the founding assistant principal of South County Secondary School in recognition of her exceptional leadership. She was also named as the founding principal of South County Middle School, something that the community was very involved with making happen, where she built a culture of integrity and cultivated strong relationships with students, teachers, and fellow administrators.

Among the many accolades earned throughout her career, Marcia received the Nancy F. Sprague Outstanding First Year Principal Award in 2013, from Fairfax County Public Schools. Truly a beacon of hope and optimism for all who knew her, Marsha dedicated herself to helping others reach for potential inside themselves and found great meaning in nurturing young minds as a revered educator and administrator.

Countless people were inspired by her wisdom and guidance throughout her esteemed life and career. She truly was a wise, empowering, and fierce protector of her teachers. She was an advocate for public education and truly a visionary. Her professional legacy will be that of excellence and devoted service to young people in Fairfax County.

Her impact as a mentor, leader, and manager, frankly, will be generationally impacting all of us. We are forever grateful for the time we received with such an amazing role model, leader, mother, teacher, wife, whose memory will always inspire us to keep moving forward with determination and grace.

The second person I wanted to acknowledge, her passing was Millie Stanges. In July, we recognized Millie as our community champion for a dedication and tireless effort to enhance our local parks and recreational facilities. A former resident of Holland Hills community, Millie's unwavering advocacy and passion have positively impacted the Mount Vernon community.

She had an intense love for the game of pickleball and served as USA Pickleball Ambassador and an advisor to the Fairfax County Advocates for Pickleball. Thanks to her determination and energy, Mount Vernon became the Pickleball capital of Fairfax County. Millie made sure that happened. I can tell you, she was at our doorstep I don't know how many times.

Millie's efforts have provided residents with a wonderful way to stay active and connected, enhancing both physical and mental well-being. Beyond Pickleball, Millie's volunteer spirit shines in her commitment to social, civic, and business causes. She has a passion for engaging with people, promoting community involvement, advocating for women's professional development.

After a long career as a public affairs manager for many large corporations, Millie served as a volunteer consultant to the Public Leadership Education Network to help educate and really inspire and engage our young people. Millie's dedication to community and personal growth have had a lasting impact on all of us.

Thank you, Millie, for rallying our community through Pickleball and so many other ways. Thank you very much. Supervisor Stork, others who would like to be recognized. Supervisor Walkinshaw to be followed by Supervisor Lusk. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I'm sad to share the passing of Diane Hoffman from brain cancer on August 29th. Diane served for more than 30 years with the Northern Virginia Soil and Water Conservation District. She retired as the Executive Director in 2012.

She was widely recognized across the region for her expertise in natural resource preservation and her extensive knowledge of stormwater management and water quality issues. She was recognized by this board in 2012 for her service with the Soil and Water Conservation District, and the district renamed its highest award as the Diane Hoffman Cooperator of the Year Award in honor of her legacy of cooperation and recognition of the belief that partnerships and cooperative efforts are the best way to solve problems and implement solutions.

She was a founding member of the Braddock Land Use and Environment Committee in 2013 and served many terms as secretary, membership chair, chair of various subcommittees because of her expertise in outreach, leadership, and coordination.

And she was usually the person who, at the end of the day, was tasked with writing the committee's resolution, making a recommendation to me because she was the person who really could bring everybody together. She was a longtime resident of the Braddock District in Red Fox Forest.

And we also recognized her as Lady Fairfax in 2022. She was one of those people who anytime there was an award that needed to be given out, I would say Diane should get that award. And turns out she had received it many, many times, many years ago, deservedly so. She was involved with the Center for Watershed Protection Board as a governance chair and vice president, the Audubon Naturalist Society, the Red Fox Forest Garden Club and various 4-H clubs and associations.

She received the Award for Conservation from the Audubon Society, the Chafin Award from the district, the Sally Ormsby Environmental Stewardship Award from the Park Authority. She was commissioned as a member, and this is one we haven't heard before, of the Ancient Order of the Chamory by the governor of Guam for her community service while she lived for two years in Guam while her husband, Carl, was stationed there.

So she made a difference in Fairfax County and Guam. She's received many, many resolutions of recognition from our board, the General Assembly, different friends groups, and different county agencies. Diane and a lot of board members knew her or met her, saw her.

She was warm and friendly, had an infectious smile. She had a skill of asking pointed questions, but not coming across as overly harsh when she did it. I'm working on that still. But Diane really could do it.

Diane was one of the original members of our task force on Lake Akatink and was able to participate in the first couple of meetings, unfortunately. Her illness took her from the task force's business, but that's part of her legacy as well, because she made contributions in just those two meetings.

Diane leaves behind her husband, Carl Hoffman, who's a retired naval officer, and their two children, Stephen and Karen, and four grandchildren. So I ask that we just keep the Hoffman family in our thoughts and prayers. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you, Supervisor Walkinshaw, and I had not heard that Diane had passed, and I, you know, I think not only did she receive a lot of awards, but if you go around this county, you can literally see the product of her work.

I can remember a time, this was a long time ago, back in the 90s, when we were starting. We hadn't really done stream restorations. We were trying to get one going in the Franconia District, and the Army Corps of Engineers was in our way. And we could get no movement from them until Diane hatched a plan, took on the Army Corps of Engineers in a very delightful way.

And they left the meeting feeling like they had accomplished something. And in reality, we had accomplished being able to do one of the first stream restorations in certainly in that end of the county and would not have happened without Diane and the work that she did, you know, for the environment and for the planet.

And so thank you for for recognizing her. But I can think of many, many projects she worked on all over this county that are thriving, have created environmental treasures because of her work and advocacy. So, thank you. Supervisor Lusk. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I want to join you in the remembrance of Gay Shane, just an amazing person who had committed her life in so many ways to the service of others. And to have her succumb to cancer is just a tough and difficult thing after 85 years.

I'll just note she grew up in Caldwell, New Jersey, but she was a longtime resident of Frank County District. Strong advocate, as I said earlier, and the chairman did as well, for the most vulnerable members of our community. She fostered so many kids and gave them a loving and caring home.

The chairman mentioned Board of Directors for Operation Renewed Hope, working to end veteran homelessness. And a strong advocate for that, as well as her work with helping treat opportunities for individuals with disabilities. So I could go on here a lot, but just really appreciate her as a person.

and she always made time to stop, talk, check in, and make sure that everyone was okay. So I know this is very difficult for our family and the broader community, but I want them to know that we're all here and acknowledging her loss and recognizing that she will be missed dearly.

Second, Mr. Chairman, this is difficult and with a bit of a heavy heart as well. I want to make the announcement of the passing of Joseph Joe Patrick Burns, who passed away last week at the age of 59. Joe enlisted in the Navy out of high school.

He was stationed across the world with his wife, Linda, and his daughter, Heather. He and his family moved to Virginia in 1980, 1999, where he at the time became commander of the Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 7327 in Springfield, where he served for over 10 years.

He was also an officer with the American Legion Post 176 in Springfield. And I had the opportunity on many occasions while visiting that post to see him and engage with him. He always had a huge smile, very jovial and just an amazing person.

And he was a vital part of our community. He will definitely be missed. His funeral services will be held at the Holy Spirit Catholic Church in Annandale at 10 a.m. on Monday, September 16th. The family has requested that in lieu of flowers, that donations be made in his honor to the VFW post 7327 or to the American Legion post 176.

And we will be keeping his family and he in our thoughts and prayers. And then finally, Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the very specific words about Chief Jonathan Woods, and I acknowledge his contributions in so many ways.

The one thing I'll share is that I got to see the tribute that was done by Fire and Rescue where they went to see him basically while he was in the ICU. So each unit of the Fire and Rescue Department stopped to salute him while he watched from his room in the hospital, and that was just an amazing thing to see, and it just tells us how much he is meant to the community.

And again, I want to keep he and his family in my thoughts and prayers during this time. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you very much, Supervisor Lusk. And seeing no one else that seeks to be recognized at this time, if all who are able could rise for a moment of silence to be followed by the Pledge of Allegiance.
Please face the flag.

I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States of America. and to the republic for which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all. And this morning we have four presentations, and for each presentation I'll announce the proclamation and or resolution and invite our speaker down to the podium, then we'll read that, and after our speaker's remarks we will all pose for a picture from the dais.

And first up today we have a proclamation recognizing U.S. Constitution Week. And this was requested by myself and Supervisor Jimenez. Our speaker today is Amanda Fowler, Regent of the National Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution.

Henry Clay Chapter, if you and all those who are here with you, certainly welcome to join you at the podium. And at this time, I will recognize Supervisor Jimenez. Well, thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have one proclamation to read. Whereas September 17th, 2024 marks the 237th annual anniversary of the drafting of the United States Constitution by the Constitutional Convention.

And whereas the Constitution of the United States of America safeguards our liberties and embodies the principles of a limited government in a Republican upheld by law. And whereas Public Law 915 guarantees the issuance of a proclamation each year by the President of the United States, designating September 17th through September 23rd as Constitution Week, and whereas the recognition of this exceptional document, the celebration of Constitution Week,

offer a time to honor our founding principles, educate citizens about the Constitution, and emphasize the responsibility of protecting and defending this Paramount Law. Now, therefore, be it resolved that the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors on behalf of all Fairfax County residents does hereby proclaim the week of September 17th through September 23rd, 2024, as Constitution Week in Fairfax County and urges all residents to protect the freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution reflect on the privilege of living in America

with all the rights and responsibilities involved and remember that lost rights may never be regained. Thank you, Supervisor Jimenez. That motion has been seconded by the Chairman and Supervisor Herity. Discussion on the motion. Supervisor Jimenez. Well, thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I'd like to welcome our proclamation recipient, Amanda Fowler, who we have met.

Nice to see you again. Good to see you. Regent of the Henry Clay Chapter of the National Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution. Recognizing Constitution Week is a tradition that the DAR started back in 1955 and was signed into law the following year by President Eisenhower.

We're sitting here nearly 70 years later, continuing to honor our most sacred document. We often speak about our differences, but I am especially pleased that we are all here to recognize the foundation that unites us all, and that is being an American and the document that defines what that means.

I'm a big believer that despite our differences, we actually have more in common with each other than not. And I believe that DAR organizers who set out to celebrate Constitution Week understand and still understand the important role that the Constitution has on our identity as Americans.

Amanda, thank you again for being here today with your colleagues and for all the hard work that you do in our community. Thank you, Supervisor Jimenez. Supervisor Bierman. So if you haven't noticed by now, sometimes I like to bring props. This is my Westlaw pocket constitution that I got the first week of law school in 2009. I carried it around in my briefcase. And yes, I was that guy in law school who carried it in my pocket and would wave it at people when I didn't like what they had to say.

But, you know, what's amazing about this little stained, old, commercialized, I'm a Westlaw guy, not LexisNexis. Sorry, folks. Only lawyers will get that joke, and apparently there aren't many in the room. But, you know, what's amazing about this little thing is that this is it.

This is it. Right to here. This part's even the index that we founded this entire country on. What's also amazing about this, I remember I was a first-year law student, and Chief Justice Roberts came to speak to all the first years, and someone asked a question, what's your favorite amendment to the Constitution?

And a law professor afterwards joked to me that he came very close to not getting it right, but of course he knocked it out of the park because the only answer is the 13th. That's always got to be the favorite. And what's very important to remember is that the 13th Amendment doesn't come until after we've been a nation for nearly 100 years.

And I think it's also important to remember that we are a nation, we the people, the first words here, that is ever-changing, ever-evolving, ever trying to move towards the future, and yet tied to some ideals and an attempt to create a government that works for everybody that endures to this day.

So sorry to wax poetic, but sometimes it's fun, especially when the Constitution is involved. And thank you for bringing the proclamation, Supervisor Jimenez and Chairman McKay. Thank you, Supervisor Beerman. Others who would like to be recognized? Supervisor Palcic. I just want to briefly thank all of you.

I love to see six very powerful women, two young ladies here joining us today. I carry my constitution at home, which I received in my high school civics class, and it's still one of my favorite, though slightly outdated, documents.

And I love that these two young ladies are with us because it's true, it is a critical document. It's also a living document. And so we are here today, and you will be our leaders in the future, ensuring that we continue to support the Constitution and revisit any things that need to be revisited in our Constitution to meet where we are.

So I just want to thank you for being here and for inspiring the next generation of female leaders. Supervisor Stork. And on that note, the 19th is pretty good, too. Just going to throw that out there. Good cover. You kind of missed that one.

Supervisor Stork. The largest single increase in voters in one day. So that was huge. So I also wanted to kind of reflect on the Constitution and the importance of the oath that all elected officials take and the fact that that oath that we take means something, should mean something to everyone.

And regrettably, it doesn't always mean that to some individuals because they don't necessarily honor, in my mind, the oath that they've taken. But I wanted to repeat the oath that Board of Supervisors members take because I do value it, and I know the folks around this table value that as well.

It says, I, in my case, Daniel G. Stork, do solemnly swear that I will support the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Virginia, and I will faithfully and impartially discharge all the duties incumbent upon me as a supervisor, in this case, the Mount Vernon District of the Board of Supervisors of Fairfax County, Virginia, according to the best of my ability, so help me God.

And that's something that I know that I hear a lot of military folks talking about that all the time, the importance of that and why it matters because I'm not pledging to any particular individual. I'm pledging to a document that has evolved, in my mind, beautifully with the initial flaws that it had.

We've worked to make it better, and I'm sure there will be other things in the future that we find that we can improve upon. But as Abraham Lincoln, of course my hero, would say, the Declaration of Independence was like our vision statement, our aspirational goal, And the Constitution is our document that we work to hopefully inform and improve upon every single day.

So, again, thank you for taking the time and recognizing this. Thank you, Supervisor Stork. And I also want to thank Dar for being here because even though we're celebrating Constitution Week, I have some close friends of mine who are heavily involved in the Daughters of the American Revolution, And I follow all the activities that they're involved in on social media and other places.

And they're working year-round on these efforts, not just during this week. And so we appreciate all the work that you do in our community. And as Supervisor Pouchek acknowledged and really appreciate our youngest members coming here today, too, we always appreciate when our youngsters can make it to the board auditorium.

And as was said, it is a living document, and it is one that guides us. Certainly, we've taken an oath of office, but should guide every resident of Fairfax County today and into the future, that living important document. And so thank you for the work that you do year-round.

With that, I think we're ready for a vote. All those in favor of the motion, please say aye. Aye. Any opposed? Any abstentions? That motion carries. And Amanda, welcome. The floor is yours. Thank you very much. I would like to thank you, Chairman McKay and the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, for this proclamation.

I want to particularly thank Mason District Supervisor Jimenez, who didn't hesitate when we approached him with our request, and with his staff, worked to make this proclamation a reality. As you said, sir, in 1955, the National Society Daughters of the American Revolution petitioned Congress with a resolution to set aside September 17th through the 23rd, dedicated for the observance of Constitution Week.

This annual celebration was established when signed into law by Dwight D. Eisenhower, president, on August 2nd, 1956. The DAR is committed to encouraging the study of and educating the public about the Constitution and the men who framed it.

The United States Constitution stands as a testament to the tenacity of Americans throughout history to maintain their liberties, freedoms, and inalienable rights. Lastly, in honor of Constitution Week, and for Supervisor Palchuk, who mentioned having an outdated Constitution copy, and Supervisor Beerman, who I think said it was old and stained, we would like to present each district supervisor and Chairman McKay with a pocket Constitution.
And in case you're wondering at what age you can join the D.A.R., I will say that it is 18 but we have with us two D.A.R. prospective members, two future members, Lena and Arlie Miller.

All right, thank you very much and thank both of you for these wonderful gifts, excellent job and with that I think we're ready for a photo and if all of you could come forward and face the audience, I'll join Supervisor Jimenez and the board can rise.
And next up, we have a resolution to recognize Cox Charities and the recipients of its 2024 community grants for their contributions to our community.

And this was requested by myself. Our speaker today, of course, is Catherine Falk, vice president at Cox Communications, who's with us. And I have a resolution, so I'm going to hand the gavel over to Supervisor Smith so that I can read the following resolution.

Whereas Cox Charities Community Grants are funded through the generous contributions of Cox employees who donate via recurring payroll deductions and one-time gifts, and the grant recipients selected through a review and voting process by the employees themselves.

And whereas Cox Charities works to help build a better future for the next generation by giving back, demonstrating a commitment to corporate social responsibility, and has positively impacted local communities in need.

And whereas these contributions have been instrumental in providing critical support, resources, and opportunities for countless individuals and families, and whereas recipient organizations including Food for Neighbors, Computer Corps, Hope Cam, Bringing Resources to Aid Women's Shelters, Empower House, Kids Are First, and Better a Life are recognized for their exceptional contributions to the community,

And whereas Cox's charitable efforts reflect dedication, hard work, and a commitment to utilizing resources to drive meaningful change and foster positive outcomes, now therefore be it resolved that the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, on behalf of all residents of Fairfax County, does hereby extend its gratitude to Cox for their generous philanthropy and commend the recipients of these charitable initiatives for their tireless efforts, dedication and success in harnessing their resources to make a significant and lasting

impact in the lives of those they serve. I'll second that emotion along with Supervisor Palachuk. Discussion on the motion? Very briefly, because I know we're going to hear from Ms. Falk in a moment about these organizations, but you heard the names of them. Many of us are very familiar with the work that these groups do in our community and are certainly very grateful for all they do to help vulnerable people throughout Fairfax County.

But I also want to take this moment to thank Cox in particular, because as the resolution reads, these are payroll deductions of Cox employees who are voluntarily giving back to the community through an organized effort that Cox has put in place.

And I think it speaks very clearly to the need for our business community to be involved in so many of the charitable works and philanthropy that takes place throughout Fairfax County. But I think it's also important to recognize that these employees then have a say in the organizations that get these awards.

And for the folks who are receiving these awards from Cox, I hope it speaks volumes to you that the employees of Cox recognize the good work that you do and they want to make a commitment to help you continue to serve our community. And so, as I said, we're going to hear from Catherine in a moment about these, but just wanted to take a moment to share that gratitude.

Thank you. Surveys of Harriton. Yeah, real quick, I'm going to pile on a little bit on Cox because the supervisor, Walkinshaw, attended the Outstanding Park Authority Employee Awards, another great thing, and in a month we're going to be doing Digital Inclusion Week.

So I'd like to echo thank you for everything that you and your employees do for our community. Thank you. I'm sorry, Supervisor Lesk, and then Supervisor Alcoyne. Thank you. Very quickly, I'll say thank you so much to the work that you're doing specifically in the county, but also in my own community.

I've seen the benefits of the contributions, and I just want to acknowledge in the Hyper Valley community the opportunity for a number of residents to be able to receive laptops so that they can be included in access to the World Wide Web.

So I'm so excited about the work that you're doing. I just want to acknowledge those who are working at Cox, that the work that they're doing is making a difference. So thank you. Thank you so much. Supervisor Alcorn? Thank you. Just piling on, you know, this is a great example of, you know, we in the government, sometimes we get focused just on our own programs.

But this is a great example of how the community steps up, how corporate citizens like Cox step up and really help make a difference. And these organizations that are highlighted today do amazing things in our community and really do help our caring community thrive.

So thank you and thank your employees for stepping up. We really appreciate it. Thank you. Seeing no further discussion, all those in favor of the motion say aye. Aye. Anyone opposed? Any abstentions? That motion carries. Mr. Chairman. Thank you, Vice Chairman Smith.

And with that, as I mentioned earlier, we have with us Catherine Falk from Cox Communications. Welcome. The floor is yours. Thank you so much. Thank you, Chairman McKay, Vice Chairman Smith, the wonderful Board of Supervisors members. So grateful to have the chance to be here today. We are grateful to be able to highlight some amazing organizations doing work right here in our community.

And as you heard, each year Cox employees give back to the Cox Charities Fund, and then a committee of them selects these winners. So here in Northern Virginia, we're pleased to announce today we will donate $45,000 in seven grants to organizations, plus two special ones you'll hear about at the end.

So when I call your name, organizations, if you'll come down and join me, the first organization that is a winner is Food for Neighbors, that focuses on the underserved teen population by raising awareness and mobilizing communities to donate food and toiletries to end hunger.

They partner with secondary schools to regularly connect these resources and grocery gift cards with students in needs. And joining me is Karen Joseph, Executive Director. Next up, bringing resources to aid women's shelters. Through partnerships with shelters, schools, and community organizations, BRAS distributes menstrual supplies and undergarments to increase health and well-being, support economic and educational success, and aid in achieving stability.

And joining me is Executive Director Tara Block. Tara's, I think, here today. Next up, Computer Corps. Computer Corps' mission is to prepare underserved Virginia adults to realize career aspirations with foundational computer and professional skills through training and outreach.

And Donna Walker-James is joining us, their Executive Director. Next up, HopeCam. HopeCam's mission is to overcome social isolation experienced by children with cancer by virtually connecting them with their classmates and peers. They provide tablets, laptops, Wi-Fi access, and HopeCam resources at no cost to families.

And Brett Fox, their director of philanthropy, is joining us remotely because he's sick today. Empowerhouse, since 1978, Empowerhouse has helped survivors of domestic violence and their children in Virginia build new lives filled with dignity, respect, safety, and hope.

They break the cycle of violence through shelter, housing, advocacy, and education, prevention, and intervention, with more than 3,800 people served in 2023. And Nancy Kelly, their Executive Development Director, is joining us today. Kids Are First provides a year's worth of custom-ordered school supplies to children who live in poverty in Fairfax County, giving them the tools to succeed.

And Susan Unger, their founder, is joining us here today. Better a Life will feed anyone who says, I'm hungry, and disrupts generational patterns by providing children and families with food, educational assistance, and life skills services.

And Elizabeth Ford, their CEO, is joining us today. In addition, Cox Charities Grants also have with us today representatives from the Fairfax County Park Authority Foundation. We recently ran a social media campaign to recognize their outstanding employees in partnership with Supervisor Walkinshaw and thank you to Supervisor Herity as well.

So we recognize they're super employees with $5,000 grants, but we also are announcing today that we were able to give an additional $5,000 grant to their Wonder Wagon, a mobile nature exploration center for children. And joining us are Roberta Longworth, their executive director of the Fairfax County Park Foundation, and Laura Aiken Ehrlichar, the Fairfax County Park Foundation board chair.

So I'm so grateful to say we're investing $45,000 in these wonderful organizations today, and thank you so much for helping us to honor them. Thank you very much, Catherine. How about a round of applause for all of these organizations? Well done.

Thank you not only to Cox for the donations, but also for highlighting the work of these groups that many of us are familiar with, but maybe not many of our residents are familiar with. and so highlighting the work that they're doing helps our residents also when they're making decisions about good causes to support so thank you for that. I think with that we're ready for a photo and if you all could come forward with with that big check and if the board could rise.
Designate September 2024 as Suicide Awareness Month in Fairfax County and this was requested

by myself, Supervisor Smith, and Supervisor Walkinshaw. And our speaker today is Loretta Goodwin, Executive Board Member of the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, National Capital Area Chapter. The first item I have is Redacting Unlawful Racial Covenants from Fairfax County Government Property Deeds, and this is with unanimous support of our board and greatly appreciative of all your folks, all the efforts. Supervisor Lusk and I attended something recently, and it was called A History of Fairfax County's Racial Covenants Lecture, presented by Dr. Kristen Moon, Professor of History and American Studies at the University of Mary Washington, and sponsored by the Nature Forward, South County Task Force, Fairfax NAACP, Mount Vernon Regional Historical Society, and Gum Springs Historical Society Museum.

It was exciting to see over 100 residents in attendance, and Dr. Moon's research, presentation, and the meeting discussions were fascinating. In the Northern Virginia suburbs, a racial covenant in property deeds were one of the many ways segregated neighborhoods were created in Fairfax County from the early 1900s until they were declared null in 1968.

Dr. Moon and other researchers are uncovering and documenting these covenants and other segregationist tools in order to educate residents about our history. Dr. Moon presented new research on the history and locations of racial covenants on subdivision properties in the Richmond Highway area as well as throughout Fairfax County with a focus on the practice in the Highville Valley Farm subdivision adjacent to Gum Springs.

She also discussed the history and lingering impacts of these covenants and shared an online interactive map that she and other researchers created which is included in the recent online report Documenting Exclusion and Resilience in Northern Virginia released in spring 2024.

Report and interactive map document the history of racial covenants barring blacks and others not of Caucasian race from owning property in the Northern Virginia suburbs. These deed restrictions dating mainly from the 1930s and 40s were nullified by the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

This has been codified in Virginia Code 36-96.6, which declares that racial covenants, among others, are void by operation of law. Thus, even without a recorded release of such covenants, the county could not and would not seek to enforce them under any circumstances.

However, we recognize the significance and importance of removing this legacy. Dr. Moon also discussed a 2020 Virginia law that makes it easier for property owners and organizations to remove or redact old racial covenants language from property deeds and encourage folks to do so.

Per Virginia Code subsection 55.1-300.1, a real property owner can release a restrictive covenant that is prohibited by subsection A of subsection 36-96.6 by recording a certificate of release of certain prohibited covenants.

The certificate can be recorded before a deed is recorded or when the owner discovers the covenant and chooses to release it. As part of her presentation, Dr. Moon shared that she had been reviewing Fairfax County government property deeds and found some that contained racial covenants.

Dr. Moon provided a list of these deeds and has indicated she has more to share. Beyond that, the process of formally releasing all of these covenants would require the review of more than 730 often complex deeds. Some are interns in various county staff offices and the clerks of court may be able to assist with this review.

There currently are no staff resources dedicated to such a project. In response to Dr. Moon's presentation, Supervisor Lusk and I committed to bringing this matter to the Board of Supervisors for consideration. This matter in conjunction with the board matter presented by me, Chairman McKay, and Supervisor Lusk on June 11, 2024, titled Recognizing Fairfax County's Historic Black Communities, Their Preservation and Ongoing Vitality, reflects an ongoing interest in reckoning with our past to gain a deeper understanding of how history influences the present opportunity landscape in Fairfax County.

Therefore, I move that the Board of Supervisors without objection direct the county attorney to draft their standard form release consistent with the requirement of Virginia's subsection 55.1-300.1, starting with the list provided by Dr. Moon and continuing as specific and lawful racial covenants are identified by county staff or the clerks of court, the county attorney is directed to file a form release of such covenants in the Fairfax County land records.

As such, as time and resources permit, county staff, in coordination with the clerks of court, should review other property deeds to county-owned properties to identify any unlawful racial covenants so that a formal release of such covenants may be filed by the county attorney.

Update the Board on this progress annually through an appropriate means and direct the Office of Public Affairs to publicize the availability of standard form release set forth in Virginia Code subsection 55.1-300.1 and to publicize information about any workshops that might be organized by county staff or the clerks of court relating to the formal release of racial covenants.
